o: Iba el vencido y asendereado don Quijote pensativo además por una parte, y muy alegre por otra.
t: Don Quixote went off vanquished and crestfallen, thoughtful on the one hand, and very cheerful on the other.

o: Causaba su tristeza el vencimiento; y la alegría, el considerar en la virtud de Sancho, como lo había mostrado en la resurreción de Altisidora, aunque con algún escrúpulo se persuadía a que la enamorada doncella fuese muerta de veras.
t: His sadness was caused by his defeat; his joy by considering the virtue of Sancho, as he had shown it in the resurrection of Altisidora, though with some scruple he persuaded himself that the enamored damsel was truly dead.

o: No iba nada Sancho alegre, porque le entristecía ver que Altisidora no le había cumplido la palabra de darle las camisas; y, yendo y viniendo en esto, dijo a su amo.
t: Sancho went along in no happy mood, for it saddened him to see that Altisidora had not kept her word and given him the shirts; and, going back and forth over this, he said to his master.

o: Pues yo les voto a tal que si me traen a las manos otro algún enfermo, que, antes que le cure, me han de untar las mías; que el abad de donde canta yanta, y no quiero creer que me haya dado el cielo la virtud que tengo para que yo la comunique con otros de bóbilis, bóbilis.
t: Well, I'll vote for this: if they bring me any other patient, they must first anoint my hands before they cure him; the abbot of the place where he sings earns his keep there, and I won't believe heaven gave me the virtue I have so that I can share it with other simpletons, simpletons.

o: — Tú tienes razón, Sancho amigo —respondió don Quijote—, y halo hecho muy mal Altisidora en no haberte dado las prometidas camisas; y, puesto que tu virtud es gratis data, que no te ha costado estudio alguno, más que estudio es recebir martirios en tu persona.
t: — You are right, friend Sancho —replied Don Quixote—, and Altisidora has done very wrong not to have given you the promised shirts; and since your virtue is a gift, costing you no study at all, the only study required is receiving scourging in your own person.

o: De mí te sé decir que si quisieras paga por los azotes del desencanto de Dulcinea, ya te la hubiera dado tal como buena; pero no sé si vendrá bien con la cura la paga, y no querría que impidiese el premio a la medicina.
t: I can tell you that if you wanted payment for the lashes of Dulcinea's disenchantment, I would have given it to you as good as gold; but I don't know whether payment will agree with the cure, and I wouldn't want it to hinder the reward due to medicine.

o: Con todo eso, me parece que no se perderá nada en probarlo: mira, Sancho, el que quieres, y azótate luego, y págate de contado y de tu propia mano, pues tienes dineros míos.
t: For all that, it seems to me that nothing will be lost by trying it: look, Sancho, take the one you want, and scourge yourself at once, and pay yourself on the spot with your own hand, since you have my money.

o: A cuyos ofrecimientos abrió Sancho los ojos y las orejas de un palmo, y dio consentimiento en su corazón a azotarse de buena gana; y dijo a su amo.
t: At these offers Sancho opened his eyes and ears a palm's breadth wide, and consented in his heart to scourge himself with good will; and he said to his master.

o: — Agora bien, señor, yo quiero disponerme a dar gusto a vuestra merced en lo que desea, con provecho mío; que el amor de mis hijos y de mi mujer me hace que me muestre interesado.
t: — Very well, sir, I want to arrange to please your grace in what you wish, to my own profit; the love of my children and my wife makes me show my interest.

o: Dígame vuestra merced: ¿cuánto me dará por cada azote que me diere?
t: Tell me, your grace: how much will you give me for each lash you give me?

o: — Si yo te hubiera de pagar, Sancho —respondió don Quijote—, conforme lo que merece la grandeza y calidad deste remedio, el tesoro de Venecia, las minas del Potosí fueran poco para pagarte; toma tú el tiento a lo que llevas mío, y pon el precio a cada azote.
t: — If I were to pay you, Sancho —replied Don Quixote—, in accordance with the greatness and quality of this remedy, the treasure of Venice and the mines of Potosí would be little enough to pay you; take your own measure of what I hold, and set the price on each lash.

o: Éstos desfalcaré yo de los que tengo de vuestra merced, y entraré en mi casa rico y contento, aunque bien azotado; porque no se toman truchas..., y no digo más.
t: I shall deduct these from what I hold of your grace's, and I shall go into my house rich and content, though well scourged; because you don't catch trout for nothing... and I'll say no more.

o: — ¡Oh Sancho bendito!
t: — Oh, blessed Sancho!

o: ¡Oh Sancho amable —respondió don Quijote—, y cuán obligados hemos de quedar Dulcinea y yo a servirte todos los días que el cielo nos diere de vida!
t: "Oh, kind Sancho," replied Don Quixote, "how deeply obliged Dulcinea and I must remain to serve you every day the sky grants us life!"

o: Si ella vuelve al ser perdido, que no es posible sino que vuelva, su desdicha habrá sido dicha, y mi vencimiento, felicísimo triunfo.
t: If she returns to the life she has lost, which is not possible otherwise than that she return, her misfortune will have been a happiness, and my defeat a most fortunate triumph.

o: Y mira, Sancho, cuándo quieres comenzar la diciplina, que porque la abrevies te añado cien reales.
t: And look, Sancho, whenever you want to begin the discipline, for because you shorten it I will add a hundred reales.

o: — ¿Cuándo? —replicó Sancho—.
t: "When?" replied Sancho.

o: Esta noche, sin falta.
t: This very night, without fail.

o: Procure vuestra merced que la tengamos en el campo, al cielo abierto, que yo me abriré mis carnes.
t: Let your grace see that we have it out in the field, under the open sky, for I will bare my flesh.

o: Llegó la noche, esperada de don Quijote con la mayor ansia del mundo, pareciéndole que las ruedas del carro de Apolo se habían quebrado, y que el día se alargaba más de lo acostumbrado, bien así como acontece a los enamorados, que jamás ajustan la cuenta de sus deseos.
t: Night arrived, awaited by Don Quixote with the greatest anxiety in the world, seeming to him that the wheels of Apollo's chariot had broken and that the day stretched out longer than usual, just as it happens to lovers, who never square the account of their desires.

o: Don Quijote, que le vio ir con denuedo y con brío, le dijo.
t: Don Quixote, who saw him go with boldness and spirit, said to him.

o: — Mira, amigo, que no te hagas pedazos; da lugar que unos azotes aguarden a otros; no quieras apresurarte tanto en la carrera, que en la mitad della te falte el aliento; quiero decir que no te des tan recio que te falte la vida antes de llegar al número deseado.
t: "Look, friend, do not break yourself to pieces; give room so that some lashes wait for others; do not hurry yourself so much in the race that in the middle of it you lose your breath; I mean, do not strike yourself so hard that your life fails you before you reach the desired number."

o: Y, porque no pierdas por carta de más ni de menos, yo estaré desde aparte contando por este mi rosario los azotes que te dieres.
t: And so that you neither lose nor gain by a card too many or too few, I will stand apart counting on this rosary of mine the lashes you give yourself.

o: Favorézcate el cielo conforme tu buena intención merece.
t: May heaven favor you as your good intention deserves.

o: — Al buen pagador no le duelen prendas —respondió Sancho—: yo pienso darme de manera que, sin matarme, me duela; que en esto debe de consistir la sustancia deste milagro.
t: "A good paymaster feels no pain at the price," replied Sancho; "I mean to give myself such a measure that, without killing me, it hurts; for in this must consist the substance of this miracle."

o: Desnudóse luego de medio cuerpo arriba, y, arrebatando el cordel, comenzó a darse, y comenzó don Quijote a contar los azotes.
t: He then stripped himself from the waist up, and, snatching up the cord, began to lash himself, and Don Quixote began to count the lashes.

o: Hasta seis o ocho se habría dado Sancho, cuando le pareció ser pesada la burla y muy barato el precio della, y, deteniéndose un poco, dijo a su amo que se llamaba a engaño, porque merecía cada azote de aquéllos ser pagado a medio real, no que a cuartillo.
t: Sancho would have given himself six or eight, when the joke seemed heavy to him and the price of it very cheap, and, stopping a little, he told his master that he was being cheated, because each one of those lashes deserved to be paid at half a real, not at a quartillo.

o: — Prosigue, Sancho amigo, y no desmayes —le dijo don Quijote—, que yo doblo la parada del precio.
t: "Go on, dear Sancho, and do not falter," Don Quixote said to him, "for I double the wager on the price."

o: — Dese modo —dijo Sancho—, ¡a la mano de Dios, y lluevan azotes!
t: "Just so," said Sancho; "in God's hand, and let the lashes rain down!"

o: Pero el socarrón dejó de dárselos en las espaldas, y daba en los árboles, con unos suspiros de cuando en cuando, que parecía que con cada uno dellos se le arrancaba el alma.
t: But the rogue stopped laying them on his own back and struck the trees instead, with now and then a sigh, so that it seemed each one of them tore his soul from him.

o: Tierna la de don Quijote, temeroso de que no se le acabase la vida, y no consiguiese su deseo por la imprudencia de Sancho, le dijo.
t: Tender was Don Quixote, fearful that his life might fail him and that he should not achieve his desire through Sancho's imprudence, and he said to him.

o: — Por tu vida, amigo, que se quede en este punto este negocio, que me parece muy áspera esta medicina, y será bien dar tiempo al tiempo; que no se ganó Zamora en un hora.
t: "For your life's sake, friend, let this business rest here, for this medicine seems very harsh to me, and it will be well to give time to time; Zamora was not won in an hour."

o: Más de mil azotes, si yo no he contado mal, te has dado: bastan por agora; que el asno, hablando a lo grosero, sufre la carga, mas no la sobrecarga.
t: More than a thousand lashes, if I have counted ill, you have given yourself: they are enough for now; the ass, speaking roughly, bears the load, but not the overload.

o: — No, no, señor —respondió Sancho—, no se ha de decir por mí: "a dineros pagados, brazos quebrados".
t: "No, no, sir," replied Sancho, "you mustn't say it on my account: 'paid money, broken arms.'"

o: Apártese vuestra merced otro poco y déjeme dar otros mil azotes siquiera, que a dos levadas déstas habremos cumplido con esta partida, y aún nos sobrará ropa.
t: Move your grace a little further aside and let me give a thousand more lashes at least; with two more of these floggings we'll have squared accounts with this batch, and we'll still have cloth to spare.

o: — Pues tú te hallas con tan buena disposición —dijo don Quijote—, el cielo te ayude, y pégate, que yo me aparto.
t: "Well, you find yourself in such good condition," said Don Quixote, "may heaven help you. Go ahead and lash away; I'll step aside."

o: Volvió Sancho a su tarea con tanto denuedo, que ya había quitado las cortezas a muchos árboles: tal era la riguridad con que se azotaba; y, alzando una vez la voz, y dando un desaforado azote en una haya, dijo.
t: Sancho returned to his task with such vigor that he had already stripped the bark from many trees—such was the severity with which he flogged himself. And once, raising his voice and dealing a most outrageous blow to a beech tree, he said:

o: — ¡Aquí morirás, Sansón, y cuantos con él son!
t: "Here you will die, Samson, and all those with him!"

o: Acudió don Quijote luego al son de la lastimada voz y del golpe del riguroso azote, y, asiendo del torcido cabestro que le servía de corbacho a Sancho, le dijo.
t: Don Quixote immediately came at the sound of the pitiful voice and the crack of the rigorous lash, and, seizing the twisted strap that served Sancho as a scourge, said to him:

o: — No permita la suerte, Sancho amigo, que por el gusto mío pierdas tú la vida, que ha de servir para sustentar a tu mujer y a tus hijos: espere Dulcinea mejor coyuntura, que yo me contendré en los límites de la esperanza propincua, y esperaré que cobres fuerzas nuevas, para que se concluya este negocio a gusto de todos.
t: "May fortune not permit, Sancho my friend, that you lose your life for my pleasure, since it must serve to support your wife and children. Let Dulcinea await a better opportunity; I will hold myself within the bounds of the hope that draws near, and wait until you recover your strength, so that this business may be concluded to everyone's satisfaction."

o: — Pues vuestra merced, señor mío, lo quiere así —respondió Sancho—, sea en buena hora, y écheme su ferreruelo sobre estas espaldas, que estoy sudando y no querría resfriarme; que los nuevos diciplinantes corren este peligro.
t: "Well, your grace, my lord, wishes it so," replied Sancho, "in a good hour, then; and throw your cloak over these shoulders of mine, for I am sweating and would not like to catch cold—new penitents run that risk."

o: Hízolo así don Quijote, y, quedándose en pelota, abrigó a Sancho, el cual se durmió hasta que le despertó el sol, y luego volvieron a proseguir su camino, a quien dieron fin, por entonces, en un lugar que tres leguas de allí estaba.
t: Don Quixote did as he was asked, and, remaining in his shirt, he wrapped Sancho up, who slept until the sun woke him; and then they went on their way, and for the time being brought their journey to an end in a place three leagues distant.

o: Apeáronse en un mesón, que por tal le reconoció don Quijote, y no por castillo de cava honda, torres, rastrillos y puente levadiza; que, después que le vencieron, con más juicio en todas las cosas discurría, como agora se dirá.
t: They dismounted at an inn, which Don Quixote recognized as such, and not as a castle of deep moat, towers, drawbridge and portcullis; for, after he had come to his senses, he judged all things more wisely than before, as will now be told.

o: Alojáronle en una sala baja, a quien servían de guadameciles unas sargas viejas pintadas, como se usan en las aldeas.
t: They gave him lodging in a low-ceilinged room, where some old painted coarse cloths served as hangings, such as are used in villages.

o: En una dellas estaba pintada de malísima mano el robo de Elena, cuando el atrevido huésped se la llevó a Menalao, y en otra estaba la historia de Dido y de Eneas, ella sobre una alta torre, como que hacía señas con una media sábana al fugitivo huésped, que por el mar, sobre una fragata o bergantín, se iba huyendo.
t: On one of them was painted, in a very clumsy hand, the rape of Helen, when the bold guest carried her off to Menelaus; and on another was the story of Dido and Aeneas, she on a high tower, making signs with a half-sheet to the fleeing guest, who was escaping over the sea in a galley or brigantine.

o: Notó en las dos historias que Elena no iba de muy mala gana, porque se reía a socapa y a lo socarrón; pero la hermosa Dido mostraba verter lágrimas del tamaño de nueces por los ojos.
t: He noticed in both stories that Helen did not go very unwillingly, for she laughed secretly and behind her back; but the beautiful Dido showed tears the size of walnuts rolling from her eyes.

o: Viendo lo cual don Quijote, dijo.
t: Seeing which, Don Quixote said:

o: — Estas dos señoras fueron desdichadísimas, por no haber nacido en esta edad, y yo sobre todos desdichado en no haber nacido en la suya: encontrara a aquestos señores, ni fuera abrasada Troya, ni Cartago destruida, pues con sólo que yo matara a Paris se escusaran tantas desgracias.
t: "These two ladies were most unfortunate, for not having been born in our age, and I most unfortunate of all in not having been born in theirs: I would have met these gentlemen, and Troy would never have been burned, nor Carthage destroyed, since with nothing more than my killing Paris so many misfortunes would have been made amends for."

o: — Yo apostaré —dijo Sancho— que antes de mucho tiempo no ha de haber bodegón, venta ni mesón, o tienda de barbero, donde no ande pintada la historia de nuestras hazañas.
t: "I'll wager," said Sancho, "that before long there will be no inn, tavern, or inn, or barber's shop, where the story of our deeds is not painted."

o: Pero querría yo que la pintasen manos de otro mejor pintor que el que ha pintado a éstas.
t: But I should like them painted by the hand of some other, better painter than the one who painted these.

o: — Tienes razón, Sancho —dijo don Quijote—, porque este pintor es como Orbaneja, un pintor que estaba en Úbeda; que, cuando le preguntaban qué pintaba, respondía: ''Lo que saliere''; y si por ventura pintaba un gallo, escribía debajo: "Éste es gallo", porque no pensasen que era zorra.
t: "You are right, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "for this painter is like Orbaneja, a painter who was in Úbeda; when they asked him what he was painting, he would answer, 'Whatever comes to hand'; and if by chance he painted a rooster, he would write underneath: 'This is a rooster,' so that no one would think it was a hen."

o: Pero, dejando esto aparte, dime si piensas, Sancho, darte otra tanda esta noche, y si quieres que sea debajo de techado, o al cielo abierto.
t: But, setting that aside, tell me whether you think, Sancho, of taking another drink tonight, and whether you would have it under a roof or out in the open sky.

o: — Pardiez, señor —respondió Sancho—, que para lo que yo pienso darme, eso se me da en casa que en el campo; pero, con todo eso, querría que fuese entre árboles, que parece que me acompañan y me ayudan a llevar mi trabajo maravillosamente.
t: "By God, sir," answered Sancho, "for what I mean to give myself, that is the same for me at home as in the field; but, for all that, I would like it among trees, for it seems as though they keep me company and help me carry on my work wonderfully."

o: — Pues no ha de ser así, Sancho amigo —respondió don Quijote—, sino que para que tomes fuerzas, lo hemos de guardar para nuestra aldea, que, a lo más tarde, llegaremos allá después de mañana.
t: "It must not be so, Sancho my friend," replied Don Quixote, "but so that you may gather strength, we must save it for our village, which we shall reach, at the latest, the day after tomorrow."

o: Sancho respondió que hiciese su gusto, pero que él quisiera concluir con brevedad aquel negocio a sangre caliente y cuando estaba picado el molino, porque en la tardanza suele estar muchas veces el peligro; y a Dios rogando y con el mazo dando, y que más valía un "toma" que dos "te daré", y el pájaro en la mano que el buitre volando.
t: Sancho replied that he should do as he wished, but that he would like to conclude that business quickly while the iron was hot and the mill was running, because delay often brings danger; and with God invoked and the mallet swinging, and that one "take" is worth more than two "I'll give you," and the bird in the hand than the vulture flying.

o: — No más refranes, Sancho, por un solo Dios —dijo don Quijote—, que parece que te vuelves al sicut erat; habla a lo llano, a lo liso, a lo no intricado, como muchas veces te he dicho, y verás como te vale un pan por ciento.
t: "No more proverbs, Sancho, for God's sake," said Don Quixote, "for you seem to be turning back to your sicut erat; speak plainly, smoothly, without intricacy, as I have told you many a time, and you will see how a loaf of bread is worth a hundred."

o: — No sé qué mala ventura es esta mía —respondió Sancho—, que no sé decir razón sin refrán, ni refrán que no me parezca razón; pero yo me enmendaré, si pudiere.
t: "I don't know what ill luck is mine," replied Sancho, "that I cannot give a reason without a proverb, nor a proverb that does not seem to me a reason; but I will mend my ways, if I can."

o: Y, con esto, cesó por entonces su plática.
t: And with this, their talk ceased for the time being.
